weeks.description:
During this Week, I visited the Museum of the Moving Image (MoMI), where I explored Overexposed: Art, Technology, and the Body and The Jim Henson Exhibition. Both exhibitions encouraged me to think about the relationship between technology, physical objects, and the human body, particularly how interaction can become part of a visual or sensory experience.

Following our introduction to the 256 Project in Week 1, I began exploring tactile buttons as the subject of my collection. The museum visit gave me an opportunity to consider how physical objects can communicate, trigger responses, and create interactions between people and technology.

This became an early starting point for my collection, allowing me to explore an everyday object through a more intentional process of visual research.

feedback.nextSteps: Begin collecting images of tactile buttons and explore different ways to organize them. Develop a spreadsheet to document the collection and identify possible categories that could guide the book's structure.

weeks.description:
During Week 3, I created my first spreadsheet to organize the images gathered for the 256 Project. I initially developed approximately 16 categories to classify different types of tactile buttons according to their characteristics, functions, and contexts.

Bell buttons
Doorbell buttons
Push buttons in art
Buttons (musical instrument)
Chord buttons
Alphameric foam and foil
Buttons of typewriters
Call buttons in Russia
Elevator buttons
Request stop push buttons
Game controller buttons / Bemani controller buttons
Game controller buttons / Face buttons
Game controller buttons
Push buttons
Damaged push buttons
Determination test
Eject buttons
Buttons (GUI)
Button panels
Power buttons
Push button light switches
Emergency signal buttons
Diagrams of emergency alarm signs
Computer keyboard keys
Call buttons
Recessed power buttons
Orginial Pics I took
Articles / Books

This spreadsheet became the foundation for organizing the collection, allowing me to track the images and establish a structure for the research. At this stage, my approach focused primarily on identifying the different types of buttons I could collect and how they could be grouped together.

As the collection developed, I began considering how to translate the spreadsheet into a physical book. This meant moving beyond gathering and categorizing images toward making editorial decisions about how the collection would be organized, presented, and experienced by the reader.

Following this feedback, I reconsidered how the images could be connected through a stronger conceptual framework rather than being divided into numerous classifications. This led me to reorganize the collection into two sections, INITIATE and INTERRUPT, focusing on the actions buttons perform rather than the many types of buttons that exist.

feedback.text: Clinton noted that the collection contained too many categories and risked becoming simply an assortment of buttons. He encouraged me to narrow the scope of the project and simplify the book's structure.
feedback.nextSteps: Reconsider the categories and identify a stronger conceptual connection between the collected images. Reduce the number of categories and develop a simpler editorial structure for the book, focusing on the actions and functions of buttons rather than their many variations.

weeks.description:
During Week 4, I restructured the collection into two sections: INITIATE and INTERRUPT. Instead of maintaining numerous categories, I organized the buttons according to the actions they perform.

INITIATE brings together buttons associated with starting, activating, or triggering an action, while INTERRUPT focuses on buttons associated with stopping, cancelling, resetting, or disrupting an action. This structure allowed me to approach the collection through function and interaction rather than simply classifying buttons by their physical appearance.

I also developed the physical format of the book as a minimal 4 × 6-inch hardcover. I wanted the compact format and straightforward presentation to keep the focus on the collected images and the relationships between them.

This iteration marked a shift in the project from a broad visual inventory toward a more focused editorial collection. By organizing the images around two opposing actions, I began exploring how buttons communicate instructions and mediate interactions between people and machines.

weeks.title: Two prototypes
weeks.description: A field of cubes in TouchDesigner, and a pixel diamond in the browser. I kept the cubes.

process.title: Notation
process.text:
The assignment was two prototypes, from two mediums. I made both in this week. Prototype one is a field of cubes in TouchDesigner. I learned the network from a tutorial, then kept the iterations that are in the living archive. Prototype two is a pixel diamond in the browser. Squares on a grid, one pulse, five seconds.

We were then asked to pick one and develop it. I picked prototype one. The cube field leaves TouchDesigner in week 6 and becomes the performance in weeks 7 and 8. Prototype two stays the diamond.

PROTOTYPE ONE · TOUCHDESIGNER

The cube field. A box, a grid of instances, swell, flip, pulse, scatter, a wireframe twin, a camera that turns, and the network I performed. The recordings are with these notes.

PROTOTYPE TWO · THE PIXEL DIAMOND

The diamond. Manhattan distance on a square grid. A ring that leaves the center and finishes once. That pulse is then the video inside a Snapchat lens: a poster marks the image, Play starts it, and the person stays in front of the picture. The lens recording is with these notes.

process.title: Prototype one
process.text:
This is the first prototype of week 05. The second is the pixel diamond. I built this one in TouchDesigner, following a tutorial for an audio-reactive field of cubes. The recordings are with these notes.

Read them in order. Each page is the next operator I kept, what it did to the cubes, and the recording that shows it. I was asked to pick one prototype and develop it. I picked this one. Week 6 takes the same field into the browser. Weeks 7 and 8 teach the sentence to perform it.

process.title: 01 — The field
process.text:
The recording is the color walking across the cubes.

I did not start from a browser. I started from a tutorial, in TouchDesigner, because the first prototype had to be a different medium from the second. The picture I was copying was a field of cubes that could be played. Before any of the gestures, the network had to draw one cube, then many.

STEP 1 — ONE BOX, THEN A WINDOW

Tab, SOP, box. A transform holds the translate, rotate, and scale. A null sits at the end of that chain so later operators can point at a checkpoint instead of at a node I might replace. A geometry COMP holds the box. A camera COMP and a light COMP, then a render TOP. The render errors until the camera exists. I set the camera to orthographic and backed it up until the cube sat in the frame. The light stayed where it was.

Alt-N makes the null after the render. A window COMP opens that null full screen, borderless, opening size set to fill. A keyboard in CHOP, key 0, is dragged onto the window’s Open parameter as a CHOP reference. Zero shows the picture. Escape leaves it. The blue dot on the null puts the same picture on the network background, which is how I watched the field while I wired the next operator.

STEP 2 — THE GRID CLONES THE BOX

A grid SOP, about 8 by 8, is not a plane. Wireframe, W, shows the points. SOP to CHOP turns those points into tx, ty, tz. A null named for the instances is dropped into the geometry COMP’s instance tab, and those three channels drive translate X, Y, and Z. The transform scale comes down until the clones read as separate cubes instead of one solid block. That group of operators is the instances container. It is the left-hand block in the swell network still.

STEP 3 — COLOR IS ANOTHER SET OF POINTS

A noise TOP, monochrome off, is the color. TOP to CHOP, another null, merged with the position channels so the geometry has RGB as well as XYZ. The instance tab takes r, g, and b. Alpha stays out. The noise was a still image until translate Z was an expression instead of a number.

```
absTime.seconds * 0.1
```

Absolute time in seconds, times a tenth, so the color walks instead of strobing. Amplitude and offset go up so the field stays bright. Dark colors dropped the cubes into the ground. The clip at the top is that walk: the same cubes, the hue moving across them.

process.title: 02 — Swell
process.text:
The still is the Swell network. Three containers are already named: instances, color, swell. The annotate says Swell.

Color moving was not enough. I wanted the cubes to breathe. An LFO CHOP is an oscillator between two values. Sine was enough. Alt-N to a null, and a rename to swell before anything is linked, because a rename after a CHOP reference breaks the expression and the parameter goes red.

STEP 1 — THE RAW WAVE IS THE WRONG SIZE

I dragged the null onto the transform’s uniform scale and set it as a CHOP reference. The LFO runs from −1 to 1. On a scale, that turns the cubes inside out. A math CHOP remaps the range. The from-range has to be −1 to 1, not the default 0 to 1, or the top of the wave gets clipped and the motion looks broken. The to-range starts small, about 0.05 to 0.1. Frequency comes down to about 0.05 so the breath is slow enough to see as a breath.

STEP 2 — A SLIDER, AND THE NAME IN THE EXPRESSION

A slider COMP runs 0 to 1. That is too much scale if it lands straight on the math. Another math CHOP caps it, about 0.15 at the top, and that channel is renamed swell_intensity. It drives the maximum of the remap. The first time I renamed after I had already dropped the reference, the Python still pointed at the old null. The link was red. I changed the name inside the expression to the new one, and the slider held the swell again.

On the still, that is the bottom container: lfo1, math1, a rename, a null, then slider1, math2, another rename, another null. The field behind the network is the same cubes, already colored, already at more than one scale. Every recording after this one has that breath in it, whether or not the gesture of the day is the swell.

process.title: 03 — Flip, pulse, scatter
process.text:
The first recording is the flip. The second is scatter and pulse.

Swell is always on. These three are gestures. Each one starts as a keyboard in CHOP, goes out through a null, and is renamed before it is attached, for the same reason as the swell: the expression has to say the name I mean.

STEP 1 — KEY 1 TURNS THEM A QUARTER

Keyboard in, key 1, renamed flip, dropped on the transform’s rotate Z. One press was one degree. I could not see it. A count CHOP makes the presses add. A math CHOP changes the step from 0–1 to 0–90, so each press is a quarter turn. A cube looks the same after 90 degrees if the turn is instant, so a lag CHOP slows it, about 0.4, with a little overshoot. The faces travel, then settle. Negative 90 turns them the other way. That chain is its own container, named flip.

STEP 2 — KEY 2 IS A NOISE, NOT A SCALE

Key 2 is renamed pulse. It does not drive the transform. It drives the amplitude of a noise SOP on the geometry. The noise already had absTime in it. I set the amplitude to 0 and let the key fill it, so the displacement only exists while the gesture is on. A lag CHOP keeps it from being a hard gate. A math CHOP takes the key from 0–1 out to about 0–0.5. A slider, renamed pulse_intensity, caps that, the same pattern as the swell slider. Larger slider, rougher pulse.

STEP 3 — SCATTER IS THE SAME CHAIN, ADDED

I duplicated the intensity and called it scatter_intensity. A copy is not a second behavior until it is combined. The pulse expression adds the scatter channel, so the noise amplitude is the key plus the scatter amount, not one replacing the other. The second clip is that sum: the cubes leave their tidy grid, then come back, while the swell is still breathing underneath. Pulse and scatter are separate containers so I can turn the amount without rewiring the key.

process.title: 04 — The twin and the turn
process.text:
The first recording is the earlier rotate-and-pulse pass, then the grid after the camera turn. The stills are the two merges of outline and filled cubes.

STEP 1 — KEY 3 SHIFTS THE ROWS

The rows needed to slip against each other, a zigzag, not a single translate of the whole field. I built one shift, then copied it down the grid and inverted every other copy so neighbors travel opposite ways. A count CHOP loops, or the rows walk off and never come back. A math CHOP keeps the distance small, about 0 to 0.05, and a slider renamed shift_intensity sets that maximum and the minimum. Key 3 is the trigger. Multiplying the minimum by −1 makes the return trip. The first version of the lighting went dull while they moved. I put the light back until the faces read again.

STEP 2 — THE GROUND IS A SWITCH, AT THE PARENT’S SIZE

A constant TOP is a flat color behind the render. A composite puts it under the picture. The constant was 256×256 and the render was 1280×720, so the composite inherited the small one and the field sat in a corner of itself. The constant’s resolution had to follow the parent.

```
parent().width
parent().height
```

I duplicated the constant for a handful of colors and fed them to a switch TOP. An LFO, through a math that turns −1..1 into the switch index, walks the ground from one color to the next. Slow enough that a color arrives, and wide enough that it reaches the last input instead of stopping on the second.

STEP 3 — OUTLINE AND FILL ARE TWO GEOMETRIES

I duplicated the geometry COMP and gave the copy a constant material, then turned the material to wireframe on the common page. Both renders were drawing every cube, so the outline and the fill occupied the same points and one of them disappeared. A delete SOP, fed from the grid null, deletes by range: one of every two points. The filled geometry instances one set of channels. The wire geometry instances the other. A merge puts the two renders together. The stills are that merge. The cubes in the rotate clip are the result: a solid and a line, on the same grid, turning with it.

STEP 4 — KEY 4 TURNS THE CAMERA, NOT THE CUBES

Flip on the cubes and flip on the view are different gestures. Key 4, a count, a math set to 45 degrees, renamed, and dropped on the camera’s Z rotation. Forty-five was the first number and it was wrong for the orthographic frame, so the step changed until the field landed on a new face instead of a awkward in-between. One light goes black on the far side of a turn. I copied the light so a side stays lit when the camera arrives there. That container is the camera flip. The clip at the top is the grid after that turn, pulse still available, the twin still drawn.

process.title: 05 — What I kept
process.text:
The still is the final network. The three recordings under it are the three outcome passes.

By now the gestures are no longer separate experiments. Keyboard in 5 is sitting on key 4, the camera turn. Around it are the sliders, the lags, the counts, the logic, the constants that feed the switch. The background of the network is the piece: filled cubes and wire cubes on the green field.

STEP 1 — QUIET IS A LOGIC, NOT ANOTHER KEY

When the bass is not hitting, the cubes should drift, and the ground should blend instead of snap. A lag on the level, then a logic CHOP that is on in that quiet. The float channel goes to the transform, on more than one axis, so the drift is not a single slider left running. The switch already had a blend. I did not want the blend on during the hit. A select CHOP takes the logic, and the blend is inverted against it: floating, the colors morph; the bass, the colors cut. The three outcome clips are that relationship played, not a single operator soloed.

STEP 2 — THE SCREEN GETS A GENERATION, THEN A RESOLUTION

On the way out of the render I wanted the picture to feel like a signal, not a clean viewport. A noise TOP on absTime.frame, through a level, into the composite above the picture. A ramp TOP is the scan. Both have to be the parent’s width and height or they tile at 256. The output resolution comes down, on the order of 480×320, so the cubes chunk. That is the last picture operation. It is also the reason the later browser work has a glass in front of the cubes. I was already putting a screen between me and the geometry.

STEP 3 — I PICKED THIS ONE

Week 05 asked for two prototypes, two mediums. This is the TouchDesigner one. The pixel diamond is the browser one. We were then asked to choose one and develop it. I kept the cube field. The keys, the swell, the twin of outline and fill, the turn of the camera, and the screen in front of the render are the behaviors I already knew how to ask for. Week 6 asks the same field to live in a page. Weeks 7 and 8 ask a sentence to play it.

process.title: Prototype two
process.text:
This is the second prototype of week 05, and the other medium. The first is the TouchDesigner cube field. This one is the pixel diamond in the browser. A portrait grid of squares. One pulse, started by Space, finished in five seconds, and then still. The squares never move. The diamond is which squares are bright, and the bright part is a ring traveling outward.

Read these in order. Each page is the next decision: what I was trying to hold, what the picture did instead, and the line I kept. The film at the top of each page plays that page’s iterations. Export video saves one 1920×1080 pass. The stage under the film is the same math as the piece, on a smaller grid so the step is readable.

```
ANIMATION_DURATION     5000 ms
VIEW                   1650 × 2550
grid at that size      59 × 95 cells, 24 px, gap 2
center                 column 29, row 47
farthest Manhattan     76
LEAD                   2.2 cells ahead of the front
TAIL                   5.5 cells behind the front

#1C1CD1  blue
#650E72  purple
#F80289  magenta
#DFFF0D  yellow
```

Each recording is one pass of that step.

Week 05 · I did not take this prototype forward. The cube field is the one I developed, in week 6 and weeks 7 and 8.

process.title: 01 — The grid
02 — The diamond
process.text:
The film grows a filled diamond from the center, one Manhattan step at a time, then holds the shape. The stage does the same thing, once. Click it to grow it again. This page is the shape only. The next page takes the fill back out and leaves the ring.

I measured a wrong distance first and the picture read as a corner sweeping toward the opposite corner. The diamond I wanted is the set of cells at the same number of steps from the center, across or down, with the diagonal costing both.

STEP 1 — MANHATTAN DISTANCE

From the center cell, one step left, right, up, or down is distance 1. Those four cells are the first ring. Distance 2 is every cell whose steps add to 2. On a square grid that ring is a diamond. The corners of the diamond point up, down, left, and right. The sides of the diamond are the stair-steps of the grid. No square is rotated.

```
export function manhattan(col, row, cx, cy) {
  return Math.abs(col - cx) + Math.abs(row - cy);
}

export function maxDistance(cols, rows) {
  const { cx, cy } = centerOf(cols, rows);
  return cx + cy;
}
```

Center of an odd grid is (cols - 1) / 2 and (rows - 1) / 2. On the 59 by 95 artboard that is column 29, row 47. The farthest cell is a corner of the grid, 29 + 47 = 76 steps away. Left and right edges are only 29 steps away. Top and bottom are 47. A portrait grid hits the sides before it hits the top and bottom. That is what this distance does. I tried a normalized distance, |dx| / cx + |dy| / cy, so the four edge midpoints would arrive together and the diamond would look tall. It stopped reading as cell steps. I went back to raw Manhattan.

STEP 2 — THE FILLED DIAMOND IS A THRESHOLD

Before the wave, the shape test was simple. A cell is on when its distance is inside the current radius, and off when it is outside. Every cell inside is on. Neighbors at the same distance agree. There is no stripe, no gap, no X.

```
amount = distance <= radius ? 1 : 0
```

Radius 0 is the center cell alone. Radius 1 adds the four orthogonal neighbors. Radius 2 adds the next diamond. The edge of the shape is always a closed diamond of squares. The stage on this page grows that fill from the center and stops when it has covered the grid. It does not loop.

STEP 3 — WHAT I STOPPED DRAWING

A diamond outline is four diagonal lines and an empty middle. An X is two of those lines. A Euclidean circle uses sqrt(dx² + dy²) and rounds into a blob. A rotated square is one square turned 45 degrees, and its edges cut through cells. I do not draw any of those. I also stopped punching rectangular groups of inactive cells into the diamond. Those read as damage. The hairline between squares stays, because that is the grid. The interior of the shape does not go dark until the wave, on the next page, asks it to.

```
distance 0     ·
distance 1    ···
distance 2   ·····
distance 3  ·······
```

Same count of cells to the left as to the right, and the same count up as down, at every radius. That equality is the diamond.

process.title: 03 — The wave
04 — The clock
05 — The color
06 — The lens
process.text:
The recording is the Snapchat lens. The picture playing inside it is the diamond.

I wanted a poster that was not a still graphic. The printed image would be the way into a camera, and the camera would be the way the pulse met a person. A finished poster with a finished layer was more systems than one scene. I started from Lens Studio’s Marker with Snapcode template and treated the poster as a trigger, the Play button as the gate, and the diamond as the video behind the body.

STEP 1 — THE POSTER IS A MARKER

The template already knew how to recognize an image. I replaced its default marker with the poster. Tracking is the recognition. Until the camera can name that image, nothing else in the scene has a reason to appear. The poster stopped being only a composition. It became the surface the software has to find.

STEP 2 — PLAY IS A TAP, NOT AN AUTOPLAY

After the marker is found, I did not want the video to start by itself. A UI button, labeled Play, sits in the camera view. A button is only a picture of an action until a script hears the tap. The press calls a function on a separate video controller. The reference has to be assigned, and playVideo has to exist on that component’s API, or the label does nothing.

```
//@input Component.ScriptComponent videoController

script.api.onPressed = function() {
    script.videoController.api.playVideo();
};
```

STEP 3 — THE VIDEO SITS BEHIND THE PERSON

I did not want the diamond pasted on top of the camera. I wanted the person standing inside it. Person segmentation builds a mask: the figure in front, the room behind. That mask does not, by itself, put a video in the room. A screen image takes the video texture and fills the view. Rendering order, the material, and the mask have to agree, or the video covers the body or never shows. The diamond is that texture. The same pulse, one play, now filling the background while the segmented figure stays in front.

The chain is the experience. Point the camera at the poster. The marker is recognized. The interface is there. Play starts the video. The mask keeps the person out of the picture that is playing behind them. Recognizing an image, showing a button, playing a file, and compositing a body are four jobs. The lens only works when they are wired together.

STEP 4 — WHAT THE PREVIEW COULD NOT FINISH

I tested in Lens Studio’s preview: poster missing, camera turned away, Play pressed, video against the mask. A working chain is not yet a finished poster. The printed image still has to tell someone to open the camera. The segmentation and the render still have to be checked on a phone. This page is the feasibility: the diamond, which had been a grid in a browser, is now a layer a person can stand in front of.

weeks.title: From TouchDesigner to the Web
weeks.description: The same material rebuilt in the browser: coded animation, type driven by music, and a VHS filter on the final pass.

process.title: Music Reacting to Type and Animation
Notation
process.text:
Read these in order. They are the notes from finding the piece out, not a manual written after I already knew the method. Each page is the next thing I ran into: what I thought was happening, what the screen actually did, and the line I kept once I understood it. The film at the top plays that step’s iterations. Export video saves one 1920×1080 pass for a slide or a page.

This set is week 6. It is the cube field from prototype one, taken out of TouchDesigner. Week 5 also holds the pixel diamond, the prototype I did not continue. Weeks 7 and 8, the sentence learning to perform, are the next notation.

process.title: 01 — The picture
02 — Typing
03 — Sound
process.text:
The film shows the failed import, then the picture coming back, then four notes and the Enter chord. Export video records the picture and the tones together. The tone on this page is the same stand-in oscillator. The piece uses the synth call in step 4.

The previous step ended with a key that already carried a behavior, and an empty place where a sound would go. I wanted that sound to be an oscillator, made at the moment of the key, with no samples. I knew the gesture. I did not know how a browser is willing to make a tone, or when it is willing to start. The first way I attached the library removed the picture.

STEP 1 — THE IMPORT RAN BEFORE THE PICTURE

I put the import at the top, because that is where every example puts it. I did not know an import runs before any line of mine. When the file failed, nothing after it ran. The canvas never got a first frame. What I saw was the green body from the first step, and I asked whether the cubes had been removed. They were still in the file. The frame had never been asked to draw. The flat green meant what I had learned it means. I went looking for a crash instead of redrawing the grid.

```
let playSound = () => {};
import('./sound.js')
  .then((sound) => {
    playSound = sound.playSound;
    sound.bootSound();
  })
  .catch((error) => {
    console.error(error);
  });
```

The fix was to let the picture start, and to load the sound after. playSound begins as a function that does nothing. I needed a stand-in so a key during the load would still type and still move the grid, and simply have no tone, instead of calling something that does not exist yet. import() with the parentheses is a function, so it can happen later. It returns a promise, which is a value that will become the module. When it arrives I replace the empty function and boot the synth once. If it fails, I log the error and the cubes are already on screen. I had to separate “the picture starts” from “the sound arrives.” Before this they were the same event, and the second one was allowed to cancel the first.

STEP 2 — A SERVER, BECAUSE A FILE ADDRESS CANNOT LOAD THIS

I tried to open the page by double-clicking the file. The modules did not load. A file address is not allowed to fetch the other files. I needed a server, and I did not have the one people usually mean. There is no bundler here, and Node was not installed. Python was, from other work. I had not thought of it as a way to serve a page.

```
python3 -m http.server 5173
```

python3 is the interpreter. -m means run a library module as a program, so I am not writing a server, I am starting one that already exists. http.server serves whatever folder I am standing in. 5173 is a port I picked. The address is http://127.0.0.1:5173. I put that same line in the start script so I would not have to remember it. The synth file ends in .mjs. I learned that the server has to describe that suffix as JavaScript, or the browser refuses the import. This one does. If it had sent the file as a generic download, the module would have failed and I would have been back at the green page, blaming the synth.

```
<script type="importmap">
{ "imports": { "@strudel/web": "./vendor/strudel-web.mjs" } }
</script>
```

The library is imported by its package name, @strudel/web. Nothing on this page knows how to turn that name into a file. I did not know the word import map until the bare name failed. The map is a small dictionary in the page: this name means this file. I copied the build into the folder so the piece does not reach out to the network while it is running. Vendored, here, just means the file lives with the work.

STEP 3 — A KEY IS NOT A CLICK

The import succeeded and the keys were still silent. I assumed the notes were wrong and I spent time on the pitches. The browser will not start audio until a gesture, and the library’s own unlock was waiting for a click. My gesture is a key. A click never comes. The context stays suspended, which is a state I had to print out before I believed the synth was fine and the permission was the problem.

```
const ctx = getAudioContext();
if (ctx.state !== 'running') await ctx.resume();
```

On the key that is about to play, I ask for the audio context and, if its state is anything other than running, I resume it. The keydown is the gesture the browser was waiting for. I had been giving it the wrong kind. After the first successful key, later keys find the context already running and this line does almost nothing. I left it there anyway, because a browser can suspend the context again when the tab is quiet.

STEP 4 — NOTES WERE REPLACING EACH OTHER

When a tone finally came out, each new letter cut off the one before it. I was using the library’s pattern player. It holds one pattern, and starting another replaces it. I had thought a word would be a sequence inside that player. A word, the way I am typing it, is several notes alive at once. I had to find the call that starts one note and leaves the others alone.

```
await superdough(
  { ...params, duration },
  ctx.currentTime + 0.02,
  duration,
);
```

superdough is that one-shot. I am still learning its arguments by hearing them miss. params is the oscillator, the envelope, the note, and the pan. The spread copies that object so I can set duration on the copy and leave the voice in the table alone. The second argument is when, on the audio clock, which is not the page clock. I add 20 milliseconds because “now” was already late. The note was being scheduled into a moment the audio renderer had passed, and it never spoke. The third argument is how long. Enter carries notes: ['c3', 'g3']. One call turned out to be one pitch. I loop the list and start one superdough per note, and only then is it a chord. I did not have the chord until I heard a single call play only the first of the two.

STEP 5 — THE WAVEFORM FOLLOWS THE GESTURE

I did not design six instruments and then attach them. The gestures already had names from the grid. I listened for which of the four basic waveforms felt like which gesture, and I changed the numbers when a vowel came out sounding like a consonant. The behavior picks the voice. The letter picks the pitch. Two vowels can swell the same way and still not be the same note. That split was the whole idea, and the numbers took longer than the idea.

```
const pitches = ['c3','d3','f3','g3','a3','c4','d4','f4','g4','a4','c5','d5'];

swell:   s 'sine'     duration 0.70   cutoff 1400   room 0.42
flip:    s 'square'   duration 0.20   cutoff 980    room 0.14
pulse:   s 'triangle' duration 0.34   cutoff 1700   room 0.24
scatter: s 'sawtooth' duration 0.24   cutoff 2600   room 0.18
shift:   s 'triangle' duration 0.48   cutoff 760    room 0.32
rotate:  s 'sine'     duration 0.85   cutoff 1100   room 0.50
```

s is the waveform. I only had four to try: sine, square, triangle, sawtooth. Sine for the gestures that open and settle, swell, and a longer sine for rotate. Square for flip. The first square was a beep that sat there, so I cut the sustain until it was a tick. Triangle for pulse. Triangle again for shift felt too close, so I dropped the cutoff to 760 and let it last longer. Cutoff I had to learn as the filter’s frequency. Lower is duller. Sawtooth for scatter was harsh the first time, so the gain sits at 0.09. Room is the reverb send. I added it when the dry oscillators felt like they were inside the laptop, not in the room with the picture.

The pitch row left E and B out only after I heard a typed word go chromatic and busy. C D F G A, across three octaves, is the row I could stand to hear in a sentence. I am not sure it is finished. It is the row that stopped irritating me.

```
pitches[(code - 97) % pitches.length]
```

I did not want to type out a note for all twenty-six letters. charCodeAt gives me the number the letter already is. “a” is 97. Subtract that and a is 0, b is 1, and the index walks the row. % 12 sends m back to the start, to c3. I was using the wrap as a convenience. I did not yet know a remainder in this language can come back negative. That shows up later, in the color clock, and it takes the picture down. Here the codes stay positive, so the wrap behaves. Digits subtract 48, which is the code for “0”. A comma is in neither range, so it falls through to e4, on the pulse voice. That e4 is the one pitch outside the row. It is what punctuation does until I decide it should do something else.

```
return 0.18 + ((code * 17) % 64) / 100;
```

Everything was in the center, and a word felt like one point in the room. If I pan by the letter’s place in the alphabet, a through z walks from left to right, which I could hear as a pattern I did not want. I multiply the character code by 17 and wrap at 64. I am not precious about 17. It does not line up with 26, so the scramble does not repeat on the octave of the alphabet. Divide by 100 and add 0.18, and the result stays between about 0.18 and 0.82. In this synth, 0 is hard left and 1 is hard right. I tried those. A letter jumping to the edge sounded like a mistake, so the offset stays modest.

STEP 6 — BACKSPACE IS THE EXCEPTION

```
s: 'square', note: 'c6', gain: 0.07, duration: 0.06, room: 0
```

Backspace was going through the pitch row and playing a full note for a delete. I heard it once and it was wrong. It does not move a cube, so it should not get a letter’s voice. It skips the lookup. A fixed short square on c6, gain 0.07, no room, about 60 milliseconds. I made it smaller until the delete answered and got out of the way.

feedback.text: Clinton told me to rethink my animation as a live performance site rather than a single, one time experience. Instead of the animation and sound completing one cycle after a phrase such as “hello world” is typed, the code should operate in a continuous, looping sequence, progressing phrase by phrase while the visuals and sound continue to respond to the user's input.He also suggested expanding the system's parameters to give users more control over the sound, such as adjusting pitch and introducing other sonic variations. Rather than using Strudel as the sound engine, he recommended exploring Tone.js, specifically its FM Synth example, as a starting point for generating sound.This feedback shifts the project toward a more open ended, performative experience, where typing becomes an ongoing interaction between language, sound, and visuals.
feedback.nextSteps: For next week, I will focus on developing the looping sequence and exploring the sound parameters. Revising the animation itself will be addressed in the following iteration.

These pages are weeks 7 and 8, written the same way: notes from finding the piece out, not a manual written after the method was already known. Each page is the next thing I ran into, what I thought was happening, what the screen actually did, and the line I kept. The film at the top plays that page’s iterations. process.title: 02 — The voice
03 — The dials
process.text:
The film builds the four dials under the sentence, one row at a time, at the values the voice starts with. Then the Pitch thumb travels to +7 and its readout follows. A second card, the voice that is actually sounding, stays at 0 the whole time. The panel under the film does the same thing live.

The FM patch had numbers, and they lived in the file. I could change them by editing, and then I could hear the result the next time I loaded the page. That is how I built the instrument. It is not how I would play it. I wanted four of those numbers in reach while a phrase was already looping, and I wanted the names to be sayable. A performer should not have to remember the word modulationIndex in the middle of a sentence.

STEP 1 — PITCH MOVES THE ROW, IT DOES NOT REPLACE IT

The letters already choose the notes, the row from week 6. If the slider picked a new note, “Go” would stop meaning those pitches, and the sentence would stop being the score. I wanted the whole row to step up or down together, the way a singer lifts a tune without changing the words.

```
pitch: { min: -12, max: 12, step: 1 }   // starts at 0
detune = pitch * 100
```

The slider is in semitones. Twelve down is an octave below, twelve up is an octave above, and zero is the letter as written. Tone’s detune is in cents. A cent is a hundredth of a semitone, so the translation is × 100. A slider at +7 becomes 700 cents, a fifth up. I write that onto the voice’s detune, and onto the options the next note will inherit, and I ramp it over 80 milliseconds so the change is a glide and not a click. The readout shows +7, −3, or 0. The letter on the plate does not change.

STEP 2 — VOLUME IS A FRACTION OF A CEILING

```
volume: { min: 0, max: 1, step: 0.01 }  // starts at 0.7
gain = volume * 0.4
```

The slider is a fraction, and the readout is the percent, so 0.7 reads 70%. The Gain node receives that fraction times 0.4. At the default the node sits at 0.28. I picked 0.4 as the loudest this one voice is allowed to be, because I already knew I might want more than one voice later, and I did not want the first voice alone to be near the edge of what the speakers can hold. Zero has to be a real silence. I ramp the gain in a straight line. An exponential ramp cannot arrive at zero. It approaches, and Tone will refuse the destination. A linear ramp may land on zero. Eighty milliseconds again, so pulling the slider down does not pop.

STEP 3 — HARMONICS IS HOW HARD THE MODULATOR PUSHES

```
harmonics: { min: 0, max: 20, step: 0.1 }  // starts at 12.2
modulationIndex = harmonics
```

This is the modulation index from the previous step, given a name I can say. At 0 the carrier is almost alone. The tone is simpler. 12.2 is the patch I kept from the example, the sound of the piece before I touch anything. I stop the slider at 20. Past that the tone gets harsh, and it gets louder in a way the volume slider is no longer honestly describing, because the new harmonics themselves carry energy. The readout keeps one decimal, so 12.2 stays 12.2 and does not become 12.20 or 12. The units are “positive” in Tone’s terms, which means zero is allowed and the ramp toward it is linear. I can pull harmonics all the way down.

STEP 4 — LENGTH STRETCHES THE NOTE AND THE WAY IT LEAVES

```
length: { min: 0.5, max: 2, step: 0.05 }  // starts at 1
noteDuration = letterDuration * length
decay = 0.2 * length
release = 0.4 * length
```

Flip was already a short square, and rotate was already a long sine, back in the week 6 voices. I did not want the slider to give every letter the same length. I wanted a multiplier. It runs from half as long to twice as long, and it starts at 1, which reads 1.0×. I multiply the note the phrase asks for, and I also multiply the envelope’s decay and release, whose home values are 0.2 and 0.4 seconds. A flip is still shorter than a swell. Both get longer when the slider moves right, and both get tighter when it moves left. I clamp the sounding duration between 0.05 and 2.2 seconds so a doubled rotate cannot become a note that outlives the phrase it belongs to by too much.

STEP 5 — THEY SIT UNDER THE SENTENCE

The plate was fixed in the upper right, a label on the picture. The dials belong to that sentence, so I put them in the same column, directly underneath, the same width. The plate stays translucent, 0.22, the way the typing step made it. The dials do not. White type on 0.22, over the white edges of the cubes, disappeared. I made the dial ground 0.72, the same border, the same monospace. Each row is the name, the range, and the readout: a grid of three columns. Start and Stop stay where they were, lower left. I did not add a fifth control, and I did not restyle the field.

STEP 6 — THE FINGER WAS THE COMMIT

The first wiring wrote the synth on every input event. I touched Pitch, and the loop I was listening to changed pitch before I had decided I wanted that. The readout and the voice were the same number. For a performance that is too fast. I am allowed to try a sound in my hand before it joins the piece. So the input handler on this page, and in the piece after this step, only writes the readout.

```
input.addEventListener('input', () => {
  readout.textContent = format(Number(input.value));
});
```

format is the small translation: semitones get a plus when they are positive, volume becomes a percent, harmonics keep one decimal, length gets the ×. The sounding voice is somewhere else, holding the numbers it had when it began. How those numbers get from the hand into a voice is the next page. I thought the answer was a button that replaced them. It was only half of the answer.
